prompt: How do GameCube/Wii projects recover per-translation-unit compiler flags and #pragmas when one game mixes objects built with different flags (e.g. -O4,p vs -O4,s, -inline, -sdata thresholds, optimize_for_size, scheduling off): which binary signals (literal pools, .sdata2 float constant duplication, string pool layout, alignment padding, sbss/sdata split, function ordering) predict a unit boundary or a flag change, and how is a flag hypothesis validated on units whose boundaries are already known? For every claim give the primary source (repo file, issue, PR, compiler manual) and state it as a falsifiable prediction: 'with X, mwcc emits Y; with X', it emits Y''. Mark anything unverified.

query: What measurements have decomp projects actually published showing which compiler flag differences between translation units in the same GameCube or Wii game produced a different instruction sequence, data layout or section placement, and how were those differences confirmed against the original binary?

Why does changing a single compiler option for one source file shift the order of data, constants and string literals in the output, and what chain of compiler decisions causes the final binary's layout to differ from the original?

What happens when a decompilation team guesses per-file compiler flags and gets a function or data section that matches the original bytes by coincidence, and how do they discover later that the guess was wrong?

Why does the Metrowerks compiler place float constants, string literals and small data in particular sections and orders, duplicating or merging them per translation unit, and how do the small-data size threshold, the optimize-for-size pragma, the scheduling pragma and the inlining settings change that layout and the instruction order in a way a person could use to work backward from the binary?

Why does a decompilation project that guesses compiler settings from the output of an x86 build of the same compiler family sometimes get the wrong answer on the PowerPC target, and what differences in how the two targets place constants, small data and alignment cause it?

What happens when a file is rebuilt with the wrong small-data size limit or the wrong optimize-for-size and scheduling settings, and how do the resulting data placement and instruction order differ from the original in a way someone could detect?

When do the binary signals used to guess a unit boundary or a flag change become ambiguous or misleading, for example because of linker deduplication, section merging, inlined functions from headers, pooled strings shared across units, or the same flags producing different layouts depending on code content, and what does a wrong hypothesis look like when checked against units whose boundaries are already known?

What measured false-positive and false-negative rates do studies report when tools try to recover where one compiled source file ends and the next begins in a stripped binary, and what happens to those rates when the linker has merged identical functions or shared string data?

At what point does tuning compiler flags to match a target binary stop converging, and what does the failure look like when the real cause is different source code or a different compiler version rather than a wrong option?

Which GameCube or Wii games have units whose original build flags contradict the common assumption that one flag set applies to the whole game or to whole libraries, such as SDK code, middleware or later patches compiled with a different compiler version, and what in the binary revealed it?

Which decompilation projects for GameCube or Wii games found that a few files, such as SDK or middleware code, only matched with a different compiler version than the rest of the game, and who reported it and how did they notice?
Why does a different release of the same compiler produce different instruction ordering, register allocation, or data and string placement for identical source code and identical options?

learning: [DERIVED][MEDIUM] A project can sit at 90 percent function coverage and still fail to link the final binary because of data layout, literal pools, or one stubborn function. So function-level progress figures overstate how close a decomp is to a verified result, and data and section placement need their own tracking. — Capacidad: You can stop equating a high function-match percentage with a finished project, and budget separately for data layout and final linking work. — Evidencia: S3 gives the 90 percent coverage example as an illustration of data layout blocking linking, not as a measured figure from a named project. — Ledger: C3 (S3)

[DERIVED][LOW] The compiler can be told to stop after any stage and hand back that stage's output: preprocessed source, assembler code, or an unlinked object file per source file. Comparing these for the single changed file, before and after the option change, isolates whether the data, constants and string literal ordering shifted at compile time or only later at link time. — Capacidad: You can request an inspectable intermediate artifact (assembly or preprocessed output) for the one file whose option changed, so a layout dispute is settled by comparing evidence rather than by debate. — Evidencia: S5 and S6 describe stop-after-stage options producing preprocessed code, assembler files, or per-file object files; the isolation strategy is my inference, not stated in the contents. — Ledger: C5 (S5)

[DERIVED][LOW] The compiler offers path-remapping options so that references to the build directory recorded in output are rewritten as if the files lived elsewhere, and the manual explicitly names this as the way to make location-independent reproducible builds. Build location is therefore one input that can change what gets embedded in the binary, and it can be neutralized. — Capacidad: You can require reproducible-build settings when you need the same source to yield the same binary, rather than accepting layout and embedded-path differences as unavoidable noise. — Evidencia: The current GCC manual (S5) explicitly describes the file-prefix-map option as usable for reproducible, location-independent builds. — Ledger: C6 (S5)

[DERIVED][HIGH] Matching every function in a file does not show the rebuilt file supplies the right data or links into the final image correctly. The guidance is to check literal pools, section placement and data ownership after functions match, and to run a full binary comparison rather than inferring a complete rebuild from a function similarity score. This is where a coincidental function match under wrong per-file settings can hide until data or layout is compared. — Capacidad: You can stop treating a high function-level match score as proof that a rebuilt file or its guessed compiler settings are correct, and require data and layout checks before counting progress as real. — Evidencia: The Retro Reversing guide states function matches do not establish correct data or linking, and cites project integration guidance on literal pools and section placement; the link to wrong compiler-flag guesses is my inference, not stated. — Ledger: C7 (S10)

[DERIVED][HIGH] The decomp.wtf data tests change a string, a floating-point constant or a pointer-table entry and expect the checker to reject each; if it still reports a complete match, the check may cover only instructions, mask relocations, omit referenced data or use a stale build. Results should also be labelled by scope: isolated function, referenced data, linked object or complete image. — Capacidad: You can audit whether your match-verification process would catch a false match by deliberately feeding it known-wrong candidates, instead of trusting its green results. — Evidencia: The contents describe the deliberate wrong-candidate tests and the failure modes to inspect, but give no measured rate of false matches; applying this to flag-guess errors is inference. — Ledger: C8 (S10)

[DERIVED][LOW] Matching each function does not prove the rebuilt file has the right constants, strings or storage placement, because function order and literal use change how constant pools are laid out, and read-only versus writable and file-scope versus function-local placement matter. A compiler-settings guess validated only on instructions can therefore look right while the data layout is wrong, which is the kind of gap that separates an x86-derived guess from the PowerPC result. — Capacidad: You can stop trusting a pass/fail match on function code alone and require a check of the rebuilt file's data, relocations and section placement before declaring a module done or a compiler guess correct. — Evidencia: S10 says to check literal pools, section placement and data ownership after functions match, and that function similarity does not imply a complete rebuild; it never explicitly addresses x86 versus PowerPC, so the link to the query is inferred. — Ledger: C13 (S10)

[DERIVED][LOW] The source stresses that matching experiments are compiler- and version-dependent and that the exact compiler, flags and resulting diff should be recorded with each candidate rather than generalized. Settings inferred from a different target's output are therefore only a hypothesis until confirmed against the real target's own toolchain and known project configuration. — Capacidad: You can stop assuming that compiler settings inferred on one architecture carry over to another, and instead budget for re-deriving and recording the configuration per target. — Evidencia: S10 advises recording compiler, flags and diff instead of treating heuristics as universal and checking the project's known configuration first; the cross-architecture conclusion is inferred, not stated. — Ledger: C14 (S10)

[VERIFIED][HIGH] Compiler behavior, available options, and default optimization sets vary by release, target and how the compiler was configured, so the same flags can yield different binaries or new diagnostics on a different version. The practical consequence is that matching a target binary requires first pinning the exact compiler version and full command, because flag tuning on the wrong version cannot converge. — Capacidad: You can treat a new compiler release as a separate suspect from the flags, and so avoid wasting engineering time re-tuning options when warnings or output differ only because the compiler version changed. — Evidencia: Both S27 and S28 state that option behavior and the set of enabled optimizations depend on compiler version and configuration; S26 adds that diagnostic abilities improve as compilers develop. — Ledger: C20 (S26, S27, S28)
